Sentence: I put a clear coat over it and then it had a gloss finish.
Content: I love anything to do with color. Recently I started buying things to do finger nail art.  I am a water paint artist and glass artist. I was looking for something that I could use that would give me better outlines when painting in miniature.  I saw these pens and decided to give them a try.  The price was reasonable. I did read the mixed reviews. Yes, the instructions are in Japanese and I can't read them, but how many American products are translated into Japanese.I decided to try all of them to make sure they worked. I found that if you don't want them to gush out some ink or whatever it is when you try to get the color flowing, you should first take all of them out of the box. Shake one back and forth a few times and then put it back in the box with point end standing up. Then after you have repeated this with all the pens, take the 1st one you shook turn it over and very lightly and I mean lightly, press it down on a paper just about 1 or 2mm, no more, Do it once and then a second time, then wait. The ink will slowly start to flow onto the point of the pen. It starts out as white and then slowly the color changes.  You can now test it with a lite touch.  If you press hard the ink will gush out. It will also do that if you shake it and immediately use it as you should allow the ink to settle and not all be in the tip. I know from experience. Put the cover on well and it shouldn't dry out. The tip is not felt but a material that if firm and won't absorb the ink, just enough .The ink is a nice consistency.It appears to be ink. It dries very fast and on paper it is a matt finish as well as on nails. I put a clear coat over it and then it had a gloss finish. It does cover well as it is opaque. I bought another set that has the extra fine tip and am looking forward to getting it.

Sentence: It won't destroy the paper by any means if it's watercolor paper or heavier weight paper, but printer paper is never ideal for these.
Content: Hello everyone! My name is Aspen, @Paraslider on Twitter, I'm an artist and animator entering college this year, and I'd like to say I've been using these for 2 years now and they still work fine to this day. Some problems arose with the paint itself, which I'll get into later.For now, I'll start off with a brief introduction to how these pens work. Posca pens are notable for their usage in graffiti and street art, so the pen nibs are pretty much made to go through the wringer. As long as the surface you're going on isn't *too* toothy, like a broken brick or something, you can expect the nib to last a while. That being said; if you plan to use these on any kind of paper, expect the paper to pill. Pilling is the result of the pen nib being so abrasive on the paper's surface that it rips up the paper's surface/tooth. It won't destroy the paper by any means if it's watercolor paper or heavier weight paper, but printer paper is never ideal for these. The way you activate these is fairly simple-- you just press the nib down on a surface a bunch until the paint fills the nib, alternating between shaking the pen (cap on, of course) and pumping the nib like crazy until you get a nice, clean, consistent stroke.Let it be known, though, you will be shaking these pens a lot. I don't want to understate this in the slightest. You will spend a lot of time shaking these pens. If your batch is particularly fussy, hours even. When I tell you I've spent upwards of an hour or two just shaking and pumping my pens for the second piece of art in particular, please believe me there. Once that's done, you should be smoothly sailing. If not, I can only refer you to Kasey Golden's posca pen videos on YouTube for troubleshooting and tips.For clarity, I'll describe the processes behind each of these art pieces, as the size you're working on and the surface material matters greatly.1- The first painting (the side profile of my OC, grey background) is something I was able to do with just this 15 pen set, and it was my first go with these, done around late 2018. Watercolor paper, 7x7 inch size if I remember correctly, and yes, the paper pilled here and there. It wasn't at all a distraction or a major flaw of the markers, and it turned out perfectly fine. It sort of feels like eraser shavings, and if you like the texture the pilling produces, feel free to keep it! if not, it's really easy to wipe off after the paint dries.As can be seen, with just the base 15 markers, a lot can be done. If you're looking for a challenge and can work in a limited color palette, this set can take you far. The colors dry opaque and are super vibrant as expected. The coverage, especially for 3M size, is really nice and it dries down smooth and matte, no streaks abound. Poscas are renowned for their ability to create flat, sleek color blocks, so if that's your thing, you'll love these.2- This next piece (pattern background, 4 characters) was a lot larger than the first one, and was done on a 16x20 inch canvas and it was completed around a month or two ago. It's clear that I expanded the color count here, and you can totally buy different colors of posca pens on amazon for relatively cheap if you get them in packs. Individual pens, however, tend to be a lot pricier and more of a hassle to get, like 6-10 bucks a pop. Unlike the paper, there was no pilling at all on a canvas surface and was overall a much smoother experience. It took a bit of getting used to the canvas's surface, but it was a really fun project regardless.Aside from all the troubleshooting I had to do.You see, herein lies my major point of contention with these paint pens, but I'm sure this isn't just limited to posca, but all paint pens in general. I was painting this on an angle, and the canvas was stationed on an easel. Because of gravity, you can expect some of your pens to go rogue on you. They may appear to dry out or get streaky, but this is just due to the orientation of your canvas. This can typically be fixed by pumping the nib and shaking, but I will admit even after a while of this, some pens just don't want to cooperate. Some might stay watery, and others might stay streaky, and some might just die on you, and that's when I suggest a replacement. For instance, the navy blue and regular blue colors here were really temperamental, but after some deep, mindful, therapeutic thoughts such as "goddamnit, please let me finish this before these die on me" I was able to power through. Don't give up on your pens because they're showing signs of wear, because there's a chance they might still work/can be revived.TL:DR; These pens are spectacular for any artist of any skill level, but they aren't perfect and have some flaws. The orientation of the pen and your canvas affects the flow of the paint. In general, you won't see these problems with a majority of your pens, but every once in a while this may occur to a few in your batch. These are lovely for color laydown and produce consistent vibrant hues. They are definitely an investment though, so consider how you intend to use them and if it's worth the cost. These will make a lovely gift for any artist or creative!

Sentence: It was really fun to experiment with them on black paper (all the colors show up great, though the white needed an extra layer over the first to be completely opaque).
Content: I love these! It has been my first experience using paint pens, and I plan to buy more. I use them mainly in mixed media drawing, though I've also used them to label planters for my container garden and various household items. I haven't had any problems with them drying out, even after being left on my desk unused for a month or two at a time. Some of the pens spurt out profuse amounts of paint when you press the tip in, but I've only had this issue with 3 of them. I just make sure to use a scrap piece of paper to test them while they're in use and use the leaky ones with caution as once you blot them they still mark just fine. They draw splendidly and I love how the paint sticks to most surfaces.I'm not sure what the paint is, but it layers over dry media just fine. It was really fun to experiment with them on black paper (all the colors show up great, though the white needed an extra layer over the first to be completely opaque). I can use it with a layer of fixative over pastels, without the fixative the tips tend to pick up the pigment and it takes a while to get it off. The medium points work well for filling in the designs I do, though I want to get some finer points for more detailed work and lettering. I can't read the instructions, so to be safe I shook them for five minutes before the first use and two minutes before using them when they have been sitting a while, giving them a good shake before I reload the tip during use. I also always store them tip up in the box on top of my desk.I look forward to picking up some more colors and tip sizes! They're quite addictive and I love the bright colors.

Let's face it, $30 for 15 pens you can "adjust" is a much better bargain than 15 pens that will cost you $150-$200. 👍😎BTW, the pens arrived in 4 days which was unexpected.

Sentence: Another thing I did test though was using it to ink up some home made stamps made of craft foam.

The pigment load seems good though, and as mentioned before; dry true to color.

Sentence: Several light coats of a matte acrylic clear coat will ensure permanency as well for long term archival of projects.
Content: This is about as good as it gets for a high quality acrylic water based marker. I've used and abused many high quality acrylic markers and nothing compares to the Uni-POSCA PC series for quality versus price. Posca ink is world renowned for it's silky smooth, slightly chalky finish, not to mention the high opacity.These markers are excellent on paper, canvas, wood, plastic, glass, or metal, and just about any smooth dry surface can be painted. Really smooth surfaces such as plastic may need a slight scuffing with a high grit sandpaper to ensure proper paint adherence. Rough surfaces will work in some cases, but tend to eat up the nib and require more ink for complete coverage.One coat is usually suffice, but I like to apply two coats to smooth out any uneven areas, with at least ten minutes of drying time between coats. Several light coats of a matte acrylic clear coat will ensure permanency as well for long term archival of projects.

Sentence: If I layer the red and use clear coat spray / shellac, it seems to help with this.
Content: I just started painting rocks, and I did a lot of research before buying my supplies. I chose these pens because they had a high average rating. A lot of people told me that paint pens don’t work well, they skip, they splatter, they are prone to leaking, the tips shred, etc. I got really lucky with these, because they work great!  They give good coverage and I have had no issues with leaking or splattering. You do have to shake them each time you use them, and you do have to “prime” them now and again by depressing the tip on paper.The tips have not shredded at all, and are great for fine detail work. I have found that there is some slight feathering if I am working on anything less than a perfectly smooth surface, but if I use a lighter pressure, they work just fine.The colors are nice, I just wish the red was brighter. If I layer the red and use clear coat spray / shellac, it seems to help with this. I currently use dark gray river rocks, and some of the darker colors (dark blue, purple, black) don’t show up as well, but all colors should work great on white rocks.I highly recommend these pens if you are using them for rock painting.

Content: I love these posca paint pens!  I mostly use them for painting on rocks, they are opaque and if you make a mistake it is easy to fix it by waiting till it is dry and then painting over the mistake.  If you are putting your rocks outside, they should have a clear spray coat applied, 4 or 5 coats.  First coat very light to seal the colors.  I found that if I didn't clear seal them with 4 or 5 coats, after a year of being out in the weather (very rainy here) the paint would flake off.  I'm waiting to see if more coats will prevent that, plus I clear coated both sides to be extra sure.  They haven't been through a winter yet.  I don't like the red color, it is too orangy for me, but all the other colors I'm happy with.  I also use them in my mixed media painting.  As long as I'm painting on a dry surface they seem to paint over anything without clogging.  If I'm very careful I can get a thin line made or tiny dots, or be more generous to fill in a larger space.  The construction of the tip is such that they can splatter tiny splats if you aren't careful, there is a bit of a learning curve to their use in detailed coloring.  But all in all, I'm very satisfied with these PC 1m pens.  I also have some in size 0.7mm in pastel colors that are wonderful and some sparkly ones.  Different tip on them.  They all work well.

Sentence: We also spray our stones with a clear coat spray, and these pens do not run.Tips: When a pen is used for the first time, you'll need to "pump" the tip of the pen gently on a practice surface, like a paper plate or sheet of copy paper.
Content: We use these paint pens for our hobby of painting smooth river stones, and they are terrific.  The tips are firm and don't fray.  The only caution I would give is that you get the best and smoothest line if you 'pull' the pen toward you.  If you 'push' the line away from you (as you would if you're writing cursive and you are writing the letter "O"), you will get some feathering unless you ease up on the pressure.  Or, if you are drawing, just turn the stone so you are drawing the pen toward you rather than pushing it away from you.We have these pens in the Extra Fine point, the Fine point, and the Medium point, and we seldom use the tiny brushes anymore.  These pens allow us (and even our 92 year old Nana) to do fine detail work, and we love them!We allow our artwork to dry when we change colors, usually using a hair dryer to speed things along.  We also spray our stones with a clear coat spray, and these pens do not run.Tips:  When a pen is used for the first time, you'll need to "pump" the tip of the pen gently on a practice surface, like a paper plate or sheet of copy paper.  You will see the ink flow into the tip.  Then you'll need to cap the pen and shake it.  Draw a line on the practice surface, to make sure it is ready.  You will need to shake the pen every time you use it, and occasionally, you will need to pump it on the practice surface again, to get the ink flowing.  CAUTION:  If you depress the tip of the pen on your artwork, it will allow the ink to flow freely down the tip.  This will cause a "blob" on your artwork.

Sentence: In the end, there was definitely a scratch there but it was understated for the blow it took and was easy to fix with the markers in about 15 seconds.I was also able to use an aerosol can of clear coat over the finished artwork created with these pens and there were no chemical interactions, cracking, shrinking, etc.
Content: These are so good, I will be ordering more as backups so I am never stuck in mid-project without the color I need. I have used these on a bunch of surfaces, but they work best on smooth, non-porous surfaces. I have used them to sketch and illustrate artwork as well as customize shoes, cleats, headphones. They are filled with an opaque fluid of bold and bright color. During the creation process, they clean up easily. If you make a slip up, it will almost instantaneously wipe off. However, the paint dries really fast (15-30 seconds max usually) and once it does, it's pretty dang durable.On smooth surfaces will easily cover with one coat. On porous fiber-based surfaces like a pair of untreated canvas Vans I did, the color needed 2-3 coats as it would soak in. This is to be expected but these markers performed so well on everything else I used them on so I thought, "What the heck. Let's try it." Even on untreated canvas, they perform much better than any other paint markers (store brand and Sharpie) I purchased at Michael's. The other nice thing is that they get used every couple of weeks or so, but they somehow stay ready to write. Other paint markers I use have been drying up after the first use and getting them going again weeks later is almost impossible.Durability has been pretty good so far. I scratched a piece of art really bad and was expecting a bit of damage. In the end, there was definitely a scratch there but it was understated for the blow it took and was easy to fix with the markers in about 15 seconds.I was also able to use an aerosol can of clear coat over the finished artwork created with these pens and there were no chemical interactions, cracking, shrinking, etc. And that was a poorly prepped surface. I have gone out of my way to throw everything at these pens, but they perform at a really high level every time.In the images I attached for reference, the markers were the only things used on the black surfaces of the sketchbook cover, headphones and top of the cycling shoes/cleats. On the bottom of the cleats, the marker work was covered with clear coat as added protection. The shoes were well used before I did the art, so the bottoms were already chewed up and the paint laid down really well and with tight lines. In the sketch on paper, the paint markers were used in combo with traditional brush markers. The painted marker parts were the highlights (works really great for that) and the light blue background graphic.

Sentence: Just don't use an excessive amount of the paint and be sure to coat them with varnish after so they stay.All in all, I'm glad I finally caved and bought these.
Content: While these are a little smaller than I had thought they were going to be, (chock that up to me not reading the description properly lol), these are actually a lot better than I was expecting.I've used paint pens before, albeit they were oil based paints by Sharpie, and I've got to say, I'm pleasantly surprised by Posca.I'd been leery of using them before because I'd heard they were notorious for gumming up and drying out but they don't seem to have that issue if you take care of them properly. Now I haven't used these extensively yet, but what I have done with them has been enjoyable thus far.Cons, the nibs are a teeny bit scratchy and if you're not careful with the paper you use or how much pressure you apply when drawing, the markers will "spit" so you'll get flecks of little paint everywhere. Likewise, sometimes they can "leak" in that while you're drawing you COULD end up with a blob in your line work, but I have deduced it's most likely caused by pushing the nib in accidentally while you move the pen. Additionally, dependant on the colour, they can take a while to dry so you'll want to give them time to do so between coats and or just use a heat gun or a hair dryer to speed up the process.Pros, a little goes a LONG way, so you don't really need to empty them in one go and they don't really need more than two coats, if that. They work on a multitude of surfaces like paper, plastic, metal, wood, vinyl, but as with most acrylic paints, you'll want to seal them for longevity later. One feature I thought was kind of cool is that they work with Copic makers~! You can use Copics on top of them, but you have to be careful not to use too much of the Copic ink in one spot or it might dissolve the paint. Lastly, these work surprisingly well with Shrink-Dinks~! Just don't use an excessive amount of the paint and be sure to coat them with varnish after so they stay.All in all, I'm glad I finally caved and bought these. Definitely recommend for people that want to give an acrylic paint pen a try~!

Sentence: I thought maybe the cardstock was the problem so I tried the markers out on other surfaces, but the same thing happened with envelopes and regular copy paper.
Content: After reading many reviews and studying several different brands, I decided to go with these for many reasons but mainly for the paint's opacity and the pastel colors included in the set. My main reason for needing these is for calculating and writing in the daily and weekly total hours worked per project on employee's timecards each payroll; so, using a utensil that is very bright, opaque, and superior to all of the handwriting underneath it is a must. I was so excited to begin using these but was immediately devastated as soon as I opened the first one. These were not at all as opaque as I had seen in almost all of the reviews but most concerningly, they were destroying the paper (cardstock) and pulling up little shreds of it with every mark made; the first picture of mine shows an example of both the paper and the marker tip after writing with it. DISCLAIMER: I was not using excessive force or doing anything while using these that would have contributed to this happening. I thought maybe the cardstock was the problem so I tried the markers out on other surfaces, but the same thing happened with envelopes and regular copy paper.  I have not seen another review that mentions this same type of issue occurring and all of the other picture's I've seen show pretty smooth lines so I'm hopeful that this is not an inevitable issue I'm facing.The other concern I have (and can hopefully also chalk up to them being defective) is the quality of the ink in what I received compared to what I expected. You can see my results in the second picture I attached where I tested out each color and then made a comparison up against another brand of paint markers I frequently use. In each line I made using the POSCA markers, the top half is the result after just 1 coat and the bottom half is 2-3 coats VS just 1 coat of the other brand marker; quite the difference and not at all the same product everyone is raving about. NOTE: we have a Steel Fabrication company and use oil based paint markers regularly in our shop; this is where I first snagged the IMC brand marker from and immediately became obsessed. Seeing how fantastically opaque and solid their finished product is, I'm sure you're wondering why I'm on the hunt for a different brand and not sticking with using those and that's because those are industrial purposed, which works great, but because they're not typically made for artsy things, their color selection is very limited and they're only sold by the case :(  So anyways, I am going to reach out to the seller and try and get their opinion on whether or not they think the quality of the markers I received is simply due to them being defective and from there, I can only hope that they are willing to send me replacement set for free. If for some reason this ends up not being the resolution to my issue, I will follow up with an update.

Sentence: Applied 2 coats of waterproof and UV-resistant sealant.
Content: SO disappointed.  Worked with the PTA to bring a rock art project to over 200 elementary school students.  I purchased 5 sets for school use and 2 for my personal use.  I used these markers after reading multiple reviews.  Product states that they are durable and colorfast and can be used on stone.  Reviews recommended these for rock art.  Applied 2 coats of waterproof and UV-resistant sealant.  Less than a month in to a mild Pacific NW summer, ALL of the reds, pinks and oranges on the rocks have faded to white.  Even the sealed ones placed under cover (out of rain and sun) at my house have faded.  I have used a lot of sealants, and the one I used for this project has sealed other acrylic, outdoor art, and has lasted for over 2 years.  Thus I know the sealant used was not the issue.  Now an entire school is going to be disappointed when they return from summer break to see that all their beautiful art has faded.  I DO NOT recommend this product.  If only I could get my money back but it's the students' disappointment that will be tougher to bear.  :(

Sentence: They cover pencil or even ink fairly well with just one coat.
Content:
Even though I don't mind not having a nice box or packaging for these paint markers, I was very disappointed to see all 29 of them thrown together in a bag that was ripped down the side inside of its amazon packaging. Were they not individually sealed, I would have thought I'd been sold a used item. So be sure your markers come in better packaging or are individually wrapped.

Secondly, I was worried as a first-time user because when I first used opened one of the markers the tip was white and dry. I shook and shook the marker and could not for the life of me get color to come out until I googled how to prep the marker correctly as the item did not come with instructions (I'm sure they say on the markers, but they're in Japanese which I cannot read- I understand this is partly on me for ordering an item from a foreign company, but with their rising popularity they really should have instructions in other languages as well if on nothing else but the listing). However, I was able to find directions on their official website as mentioned, so I digress.

To get your markers to work, you must shake them (you will hear a noise, this is normal) and then "pump" the marker a few times. That is, if you push the tip down on a piece of paper it will go into the marker and you will start to see the paint flow onto the tip. The website said to pump one or two times but I find I need to pump it for much more than that, but maybe each marker is different. This is easy enough to do and I don't mind the prepping at all, I just wish I knew this beforehand so I didn't almost lose my mind thinking I was sold defective markers.

The colors are very bright and pop well, even with pastels. They cover pencil or even ink fairly well with just one coat. Being as bright as they are they might not work for every project, but I bought them because of that uniqueness. I have not used them much but I have noticed the tip will flake a bit when covering large areas which is annoying, so I wish they'd used a different material but I'm not an expert on other options so maybe this was the best they could do.

Overall, they're expensive as art supplies tend to be, but they're a solid brand with a good reputation. I just probably wouldn't buy them from amazon again due to the poor packaging and instructions. Hopefully they last me a while and don't dry out.

They also dry out more quickly than more expensive brands. Several colors are specifically frustrating; the blues will run if sprayed with a sealant (this was not the case a few years ago) and the oranges and pinks require several coats to fully cover the surface, as they are somewhat translucent. The colors are bright in general but some colors are dull and can appear muddy compared to other brands. These will stick to most surfaces and are pretty permanent. The variety of shades for the price make these a good starter set. I recommend only shaking the markers downward 2-3 times before pumping the paint. These used to be much more expensive, and the packaging reflects the affordability of the current product line.

The first thing I didn't expect was that they were all individually shrink wrapped. Each pen. Whew, that took some time to get them all out of the wrapping.

The second thing I wasn't expecting is that you need to prime them the first time you use each pen. The first one just flooded out onto my paper. Don't shake more than a few times and then press the tip on the paper gently! You'll still have a small amount of paint come out, but not gushing. Don't prime on your work surface, prime on an extra sheet of paper. Otherwise you'll have a small puddle of paint on your work.

The next thing is that, although I did receive all 21 pens, I didn't get two of the colors that were listed, instead got two other colors in their place. Peach and Yellow Green were not included, instead I received Pink and Aqua Blue. That wasn't a big deal, there are enough colors that I won't miss the ones missing, and will use the substituted colors.

It took a while to figure out which colors I actually had because the writing on the packaging and on the pens is all in Japanese. I've seen some that are in English, and if I did this again, I'd definitely make sure I got pens with English. Since the colors aren't readable for me on the pens, I numbered each pen lid and made a chart in my sketchbook of the colors and numbers.

When I created this chart, I found that they pill up on textured watercolor paper. This was noted in other reviews I read, so I wasn't surprised.

All in all, now that I've primed all the pens and made my chart of colors and figured out what paper to use, I'm ready to go and think I will enjoy these pens. :) They really are a good price!

Sentence:
This was 160gsm paper which can withstand watercolor markers and ink with no bleed through.

Viscosity was not consistent.
Content:
On the video I uploaded I had only used the markers to draw the snowflakes (I used watercolor markers to write “January”). You can see the bleed through on the other side of the paper. This was 160gsm paper which can withstand watercolor markers and ink with no bleed through.

Viscosity was not consistent. Meaning some markers were watery. Blending was hard, markers would dry to fast and then I would get the clumping. I used these markers on 4 different papers, I had the best results with bee creative marker paper, but still had clumpy blending.

The 1st day I used these markers I had better results than the very next day. On the 1st day I followed all the directions on the back of the box before using markers: shook, aired out, primed, washed nibs after use. The second day I shook again, some markers were still watery. I aired them out and they were still watery. I also now found that the markers were harder to blend, even on the better bee creative paper.

Maybe I will try playing with them some more, I do want them to work, but I don’t want them to frustrate me.

Sentence: Have never had any issues with chipping after drying (I do not use sealant).
Content:
I've been using these to create signs for beers on tap at my bar for about 8 months or so and they are probably the best quality acrylic pens I've had my hands on.

They seem to last quite a long time and they're extremely versatile. I use them primarily on smooth wood that is coated with black chalkboard paint but I have also used them on cardboard, paper, canvas, and plastic. Have never had any issues with chipping after drying (I do not use sealant). Signs stay pretty dry, so I can't speak to how the acrylic handles an accidental splash of liquid.

The fine detail nibs are incredible and aren't easily ruined or dulled. Distribution of paint is consistent, though when it gets low you may find yourself pressing the tip more often. Nibs are easily replaceable and washable if you hit a clog (proper storage is necessary).

The colors in the E+ pack are perfect for what I need as a sign artist and you really can't beat the price for what you get. 5/5 stars by far.

Sentence: Purchased a couple of black paper sketch pads and journals to try out as travel journals.
Content: Purchased a couple of black paper sketch pads and journals to try out as travel journals. Since I wanted to (mostly) write on the pages rather than draw, the hardest part was finding writing instruments that look the way I wanted on black paper. Attached is a photo of the results of only some of the pens / colored pencils / gel pens, etc. tried. Shown are the best of all of them and I think you'll agree the examples on the left are superior to the ones on the right. (Depending, of course, what you want to do with the sketch pad.)First the not-so-good ones on the right. Tried expensive white, gold, and silver pens from Blick / Hobby Lobby / Michaels and cheaper ones from Dollar Tree / Amazon. (I now have a fairly impressive collection of pens, pencils, and markers that won't work with black paper but will hopefully be good for other projects.) The colored pencil results are very subtle and almost get lost on the page,. Not that great for writing, but they might be great if that's the look you want. FYI - a couple of different brands of gel pens did not work at all for me on black paper. You could barely see them and once they dried completely they were even harder to see. It could have been the brands I tried, so you might want to see for yourself and your individual need.Now the good - I ordered these Artistro Metallic Paint Pens (Acrylic), and they are the clear winners (shown on the left in the photo) for writing on black paper. You get 12 pens for under $16 (sale price when I purchased them) and all of them look good and pop on the black paper with one possible exception - the black/slate pen. Maybe it would be great for semi-secret messages? There are a couple more colors (rust and turquoise) in the pack that there wasn't room for on the test page, but they're nice too. Also, these pens write very smoothly - no clumps or random gooey places like most of the other paint pens tested.I would definitely recommend these pens, especially if you want to write on a dark or black paper!

Sentence: Very happy with the pen's overall performance.I drew/painted some little rubber rain boots.
Content: Bought the 42 piece "extra fine tip" set for a project and they worked beautifully! Very happy with the pen's overall performance.I drew/painted some little rubber rain boots. The boots, unfortunately, did not stay painted for long. After the first wear, the paint ended up cracking off. I did some research before hand and thought with all the steps I took that it would last longer but it did not.Regardless, that's not a fault of these pens but of the fact that rubber is too flexible to be painted with acrylic paint. Rubber bends and moves too much so that's why the paint cracked and chipped. I'm going to try these pens out with canvas slip-on shoes and see how that goes. I'll try and provide an update later on that.In the meantime, I leave a 5 star review on these. Working in layers, the colors build wonderfully, I was most impressed with the white pen as it has a very strong opacity so all I needed was 2-3 layers to get the coverage I was looking for.The paint dries to an almost matte-like finish. The tip on these pens is similar to a fine tip sharpie. It's almost like working with a sharpie but the dry time is not as quick (obviously). Maybe a minute or two for it to fully dry enough to add the next layer.Because I was working with rubber, if I made a mistake I could just use some rubbing alcohol to clean up the mistake easy-peasy without any problems. The paint did not stain the boot or anything like that.While I was drawing/painting, I did have to pump and shake the pen often for more paint to release from the chamber, but that is the case with most paint pens, and was what I expected when I bought these.I'm also happy that they give you 2 black pens and 2 white pens as those 2 colors are what I use the most for my projects.If there is one complaint that I do have, it's that there is only one red pen out of the whole set. No other shade of red is provided which meant I hade to dig out my tubes of red acrylic paints and brushes in order to get the darker shade of red you see on the rocket. It's not that big of a deal, but it's something I noticed that could be improved. There is a surplus of blues, however, so if you have a blue based project then this is the pen set for you lol.

Sentence: These water-based Flymax Paint Markers are very vibrant on coated black papers and on top of lines made by alcohol-based markers (and other writing utensils)!
Content: These water-based Flymax Paint Markers are very vibrant on coated black papers and on top of lines made by alcohol-based markers (and other writing utensils)! I am extremely grateful for these markers, which are easy to control when illustrating small artwork. They work exactly as described when the directions on the back of the box are followed! I have added extra details to the box directions to help with anyone having trouble, especially when the pen is being used for the first time:1. Leave the pen cap on and shake the pen several times prior to using.2. Uncap, and press down on the pen tip (onto some paper) with enough force to push the tip inside of the pen. Release pressure to let the tip back out. Please do this several times to encourage the white ink to come out until the white ink flows when you write with the tip.3. Recap the pen tightly after using.If you are using a thicker substrate to write with (like ballpoint pen ink, which is actually a paste made by dissolving dye in solvent), the white Paint Marker water-based ink might sink through the thick ink a bit and show some of the color underneath. If you are drawing on top of alcohol-based markers or watercolors, the white Paint Marker may show up better since markers and diluted paints usually sink deeply into textured paper and don't leave a thick substrate on top of the paper. Happy drawing/writing/decorating! :D

Sentence: The felt tip resembles a regular marker tip, but with some finesse you can make it "Fine".Using these on cardboard, paper, and opaque washi tape worked just fine.Overall, you get a very nice assortment for a great price and should last you a while depending on it's use.
Content: If you're looking for a white paint marker, give these a try.These are easy to use as long as you take a look at the instructions before hand. The paint can get quite messy if you're not careful and may run. Simply shake the marker a few times, push down the tip and write.I highly suggest doing a test run to get a feel for how they work before each go as the paint will blob on the first go. Once you start writing the paint comes out easily and is bright. Once it starts to turn sheer or isn't as white, give it a shake or push the tip again--but carefully.The box says "Extra Fine Tip" but I wouldn't call these extra fine by any means. It's also listed as 0.7mm which isn't really extra fine anyway; depending on how hard you push the pen could vary. I would say the tip is closer to 1 or 2mm though. The felt tip resembles a regular marker tip, but with some finesse you can make it "Fine".Using these on cardboard, paper, and opaque washi tape worked just fine.Overall, you get a very nice assortment for a great price and should last you a while depending on it's use.

Sentence: I used pencil to write on the board first of course but if I messed up with the marker, I had a magic eraser handy to quickly rub it off.
Content: Love these pens! They are a very bright vivid white. I used one on a piece of plywood I had painted black to put in a frame for a motto. They were awesome. I used pencil to write on the board first of course but if I messed up with the marker, I had a magic eraser handy to quickly rub it off. The cool thing is that once it’s completely dry it’s much harder to remove, so I actually used a magic eraser to remove my pencil lines. I also sprayed it with a light coat of matte clear coat. Most of the time the ink flow was consistent and smooth. But if I laid it down and picked it up later I first tried it on a scrap to make sure it was good, which I definitely recommend. Definitely best white paint pen I’ve ever used! My motto brought almost $500 at a family auction 👏🏻 so i was glad that I had used good quality pens!

The 0.7mm fine tip allows for detailed work and intricate designs, making them ideal for creating precise lines and intricate patterns. The white acrylic paint flows smoothly from the marker, providing consistent coverage without streaks or smudges.I particularly enjoy using these markers on black paper, as the opaque white pigment stands out vividly against the dark background. Sentence: These work on light or dark paper with full coverage.
Content: These water-based acrylic paint markers are a good alternative to oil-based markers. You’ll still have to shake them and press the tip to activate, just as you would with oil-based paint markers. The advantage over oil-based is that the paint goes on smoothly with no clumps, and the coverage is very good. These work on light or dark paper with full coverage. Colors can be layered once dry.I like to use oil-based paint markers to draw or write on plastic surfaces and was hoping these would work just as well. They’re a decent alternative but they do bead up on very slick or glossy surfaces. However, the paint will stay on once dry if it is something that won’t be handled often. But if the plastic has any tooth or texture, these work very well. The paint also beaded up a little on glass, though not as much as on the slick plastic surfaces. I tried them on metal, rocks, wood, craft foam, and fabric, all with success. They also are wonderfully and highly metallic colors, shimmering beautifully with the slightest amount of light. They are easy to manipulate to get a variety of marks and line variation. I’m happy that it’s a more kid-friendly alternative to oil-based markers (although still with supervision).

Sentence: I bought these specifically for coloring wax seals but with the dual purpose of card making calligraphy if that didn't work out.
Content: I bought these specifically for coloring wax seals but with the dual purpose of card making calligraphy if that didn't work out. It comes with a decent selection of colors and the pens are double ended with a nub and a brush head.I tried them on some junk mail when they arrived and was happy with the smooth flow of the brush head. The white in particular stood out quite well, which is usually the most disappointing color in my experience. It takes a few seconds to dry so you have to keep that in mind.As far as using on the wax seals, it kind of worked, but not well. The paint spread and slipped across the wax and neither head was particularly effective. The brush head was a bit too thick and bled. The result is not something I would be happy gifting, so that's out the window.My second test was on card stock. This was better. I prefer the brush head and they glide well but were varying thickness. The nubs seem more consistent and offer a bolder line. My biggest complaint here is that almost every single color is flat matte. Out of the few I tested, only the gold had a metallic hue. This really depends on your needs, but for me, it's not the prettiest effect for card making. Will probably work best on rocks and maybe glass if it doesn't spread too much before drying.The other drawback is the flimsy box. Couldn't get the markers back in and you have to store these flat (horizontally) to prevent leakage. So provided I decide to keep these, I have to figure out how to store them properly. Hope this helps someone make their decision!

Sentence: After you are done, I do recommend not skipping the clear coat though.
Content: My backyard has a bunch of rocks.  Every time I do my yard, I end up with at least a bucket of rocks varying in different shapes and sizes.I decided to start my own rock garden and had the opportunity to give these a try.  These come with a large variety of colors and what's great is that the tips were not getting worn on the rocks, which was great as well.  I decided to go against putting a base coat on these to save on time and was surprised that even without a base coat the color was able to still pop through.  Depending on how perfect you want your rocks, I do recommend putting a coat of base coat though.  As for the lighter colors, you do have to go through another pass after drying as the dark color of the rocks do appear to show through.  After you are done, I do recommend not skipping the clear coat though.  That will help seal in the color and even add some shine.The use is just like any other paint marker.  You shake it up a few times and then compress the tip on a piece of paper or surface to prime the tip with paint.As mentioned, no issues with the color and could see you using these to even customize stickers; however, it took forever to get here.  I think it was about a month before I got the markers.  Not sure what the hold up was, but when it was out for delivery, it didn't make it until 2 days later.  Also, because of the variety of colors, I would have wished for each color to be marked what the color was as a lot look very similar.

Sentence: It could be easily scratched off glass, plastic and metal, so if you did use the ink on those surfaces, you'd need to varnish afterwards to protect it.Given their relatively low cost, I think these are decent paint markers.
Content: As with a lot of paint markers, these have strengths and weaknesses.The five pens come in a funky cardboard tube. The two largest ones are wrapped in plastic, which must be removed. All of the pens have a ball bearing mixer inside, so they have to be shaken before use. The instructions say to pump the nib 2-3 times to get the ink flowing. That's true of the smaller pens, but I found the two largest markers needed their nibs pumped quite a few times to get the ink flowing well. Once primed, all of the pens flow really well. Ink laydown is consistent and smooth.I tested the pens on paper first and found them to be really nice to use. They produce a very rich, opaque black with virtually no bleed. With the larger markers, you will notice come cockling of the paper, just as if you were using acrylic paint, so I would advise using at least 300gsm paper or card if you plan to use the chunkier markers for drawing and illustration.Using the pens on other surfaces had mixed results. On anything porous, the ink adheres well. However, on shiny or hard surfaces, I did notice some beading, and the ink adhesion wasn't great on anything glossy. It could be easily scratched off glass, plastic and metal, so if you did use the ink on those surfaces, you'd need to varnish afterwards to protect it.Given their relatively low cost, I think these are decent paint markers. If you're looking to draw on hard surfaces specifically, then you might want to look elsewhere, but if used on paper, card and porous surfaces, they perform really well and are a good buy.

Sentence: The colors do show up pretty well on black paper which is a plus to me (see the doodle I uploaded).
Content: I call these "generic Chinese pens" because the box and pens don't have a company/brand name on them, and I've seen the same set for sale on Amazon under at least 2 different company names. If you're going to buy them search Amazon and buy the least expensive - you'll know they're the same because of the box design and the lettering on the pens.  The quality is pretty average for this type of pen.The instructions on the included 'instruction manual' say to shake them at least 30 times before using and I found out why - if you don't mix them thoroughly before each use you can end up with watery thin paint, or tiny clumps of paint. The description calls them 'extra-fine' - I'd  call it medium fine but they do make good lines.  In my opinion the color selection is just OK - I'd like to have a brighter green and blue than these. I did a swatch chart so you can judge for yourself, but note the colors are not numbered or named on the pens or caps, and the cap color is only a general indication of the paint color.  I couldn't get the colors to blend well either when they were both wet, or by overlaying one color on another dry color.  The colors do show up pretty well on black paper which is a plus to me (see the doodle I uploaded). On the down side these seem to be very wet paints even when thoroughly mixed and they do bleed through thin paper.  I haven't used them on rocks, plastic or ceramics but I suspect they would be better suited for those materials.  If you do use paper you'll probably want to use a heavier weight (like for watercolors or mixed media).  Because of the wetness they take a bit longer to dry than other acrylic pens I've used.Important: You'll need to prime these after mixing before the first use - quickly press the tip straight down on some scrap material and release - you'll see the nib (tip) fill with paint.  I'd recommend using cardboard as there's a good chance of ending up with a puddle or drips.  Also I'd recommend doing a line on scrap paper before actually using to remove any excess paint from the nib.  The instructions say if one gets clogged you can remove the nib and wash it out with warm water, but I'm not going to try that as it would undoubtedly make a mess.  I have yet to use these where I didn't end up with a little paint on my hand.  As far as storage, the box isn't going to last long - if you do buy these I'd recommend keeping them in a cheap pencil case (there are plenty on Amazon).  All in all these are OK pens for casual use at the current price, but if you want professional quality definitely look elsewhere.

Content:
Very much like Poscas. Some of the colors look identical, in fact, including one of the yellows, the light green, the red, and the black and white. The blues and purples are different. They seem to pump/fill a bit faster than Poscas, although they are extremely similar at a much more reasonable price point. The yellows seemed a bit more opaque. Same factory maybe?? Required little shaking to get them started compared to other markers I've used. Love them. Wish they had more colors and other sizes/nibs.

UPDATE: I bought the new 36 set and the paint seemed a bit thinner. There is a nice range of blues and purples, although they could've varied the tones (or even the hues) of the purples. Same for the yellows. When overlapping to fill a larger area, the sheen is a bit different ranging from matte to satin.

I need to compare these to the first set I got. Several colors are like Poscas, but they have unique colors not available in the Posca line, including the yellows and the cool greens. One criticism of this set is that except for the really light green, they are all blue-leaning greens. This set needs one or two warm greens. An emerald or middle-of-the road green.

It seems like the selection of colors was intentional in the way they filled in the missing Posca colors, but also careless as they should have spent more time tweaking the colors. The oranges have a lot of white in them. Similar to Posca, but too much white. This is just one example of where they needed to put forth more time before releasing a product.

Definitely the sheen, film of these markers is different from Posca. Posca's are all matte (you can feel the roughness). It took a lot of chemistry to develop this as every pigment has its own sheen (yes, some pigments are glossy and need added agents to make them more matte).

One of the markers released liquid orange paint that flew through the air when I used it (and landed on my table). These definitely seem more liquid than the other sets I bought. So, nitpicking aside, I like these.

They work well with Poscas and are very similar except not quite as matte or consistently matte. As a standalone set, the greens are lacking in hues. But for the money you pay, they're a nice addition to a marker collection.

The listing now says they are lightfast. I am going to test them, as Posca reds, pinks, browns (and probably purples) fade a lot, and the lightfast ones available from other companies don't perform as well as these or Poscas as Liquitex and Amsterdam have not perfected their paint formulas (they have been selling markers long enough to make them better quality also).

Being lightfast is huge, if, in fact they are, and it would be nice to see this company share how they were tested--or include lightfast ratings. One other marker dealer, Tooli-Art claims to be lightfast, but the proof is in the pudding, and when companies don't rate the lightfastness or the testing standards, it doesn't lend a lot of credibility to the claims, but let's hope this, that SFAIH is telling the truth and their reds, pinks, and purples are really lightfast, which makes them truly artist grade...

After using these, I was able, after letting them dry for a couple weeks, to use a brush-on, Liquitex matte varnish full strength, no fussing. Note, I was able to do this with Poscas too. The key is to let the paint sit for a length of time, not try to do it the same day or even the next day because they will bleed if the paint has not cured. One you use a matte or other varnish, the discrepancies in finish disappear.

One more feature to mention, these have numbers available on the ends for your charts. Will they be sold open stock? Would be lovely to see these in small nib sizes with nib replacements (I am wondering if they will take Posca nibs)... Great Buy.

Sentence: For instance I used one to write on the lid of a jar of pigment to label it, no smudging once it was dry which was excellent.Mostly I tested these on mixed media paper, some of the fine point sides were a little dried out and required wiping off before they would work.
Content: I have no experience with acrylic markers. Acrylic paint yes and markers of various types yes, but not this style, but I wanted to try them out since I collect various art supplies. I hoped they would behave like overly large gel pens and give me the ability to add some details over black ink or black paint, and they do that, but there is more going on. For instance I used one to write on the lid of a jar of pigment to label it, no smudging once it was dry which was excellent.Mostly I tested these on mixed media paper, some of the fine point sides were a little dried out and required wiping off before they would work. It was a learning experience, my silly illustration turned out a lot more pop art since you layer rather than shade in a gradient to get dimension (in contrast with the alcohol markers which can give you a softer edge, these want a much more harsh distinct lines) these are really not the style I usually work with, but since they are waterproof (I did an ink wash over the whole piece once dried) I could do some really fun mixed media pieces with ink and paint. There is little to no smell and they dry fairly quickly, since they can go on multiple surfaces I find myself wondering if I can add an interesting mural to the side of my boring black computer desk. I am glad I got these markers and look forward to integrating them more in my art and seeing what other weird things I can do with them.

Sentence: I've never used Posca markers before, but having recently entered the adult coloring community, I have heard others sing their praises, and now I can say, rightfully so.
Content: I've never used Posca markers before, but having recently entered the adult coloring community, I have heard others sing their praises, and now I can say, rightfully so.  This "holiday" set of 22 markers is really 11 makers of the 3 m and 5 M variety.  Same colors - just different sizes.  The colors include:  black (a beautiful opaque black) and white (equally gorgeous for a paint marker), pink, lavender, light pink, blue, orange, sunshine yellow, light green, aqua green, and sky blue.  I'm not sure why this termed a holiday set.  It is coming out near Christmas and yet the set does not contain what you might consider a traditional Christmas red or green.  (Actually, if you get the larger 62 count set, I bet there is one in it. )  It also does not have any "holiday" packaging aside the very nice hard side (?) case that the markers come in which I suppose makes it giftable.  So there's that.  But the markers themselves are kind of impressive for what they are.  The paint/ink is smooth.  It comes easily off the tip with streaking or skipping.  The color is bright and yet opaque.  I just wrote some words with the colors on marker paper and was extremely surprised by the quality.However, my one "concern" is that the markers themselves feel rather light, which makes me wonder exactly how much paint/ink is in them and how long I can expect them to last before I need to replace them.  Posca markers not cheap.  They are at the highest end of paint makers in the field.  Please see the 62 ct set in this listing if you are unsure of what that means.  I guess I just want to know that I'm getting my money's worth at the price point.  I also think that I would have preferred to have this set with more colors at the same size for the price rather repeating the 11 colors just to have two different sizes.  But overall, this is a quality set.  NOW I GET IT.

Sentence:
The white, and other light-colored markers do a great job - bright and easy to see on dark paper.

THINGS TO KEEP IN MIND:
When you want to use one of these markers, you kinda have to "get them flowing" initially.
Content:
I use markers for a variety of crafts, and have purchased way too many glitter, metallic and other specialty markers online and from local craft stores.

WHAT MAKES THIS A GOOD SET:
First, that you get so many different styles of markers in one big box that's easy to store. Anyone that has priced buying these in small sets or even individually will appreciate that.
The glitter pens are pretty glittery. I have a few glitter pens that are a different brand that are more glittery, but they were expensive pens that I had to buy individually from a local craft store. For the price of these, the glitter effect is pretty good.
The metallic markers are also pretty good. The effect is comparable to other brands I have that cost slightly more than these.
You get a good variety of colors in the Classic, Pastel, Neon, Morandi (which are "muted" colors btw, vs bright neon colors). The white, and other light-colored markers do a great job - bright and easy to see on dark paper.

THINGS TO KEEP IN MIND:
When you want to use one of these markers, you kinda have to "get them flowing" initially. They printed a little diagram on the side showing you how to pump them to get them flowing. If you're not getting a very strong, bold line, you need to pump the marker some more, to get the ink flowing better.
Due to the nature of how ink flows from these markers, you can get the best result using them if you're very purposeful in your marks. If you want to make quick, very fast marks, these may not be the pens for you.

- My biggest complaint is the box they come in. The way that this box is depicted in the product description pictures makes it seem like it arrives in a tiered, organized box. It's just a box. It's a nice box, but it's just a box, without any tiers or dividers. The markers themselves are numbered, and the back of the box has a chart or "key" that you can use, to identify what type of marker each number is.
Additionally, the names of the actual colors are not on the box, nor are they on the markers themselves. This might not bother you, but for colorblind folks like myself, not having the actual name of the color written on these markers can be a bit of an issue.

Overall, this is a good variety of specialty markers that I'm sure to get a lot of use out of.

Sentence: Even on dark paper the Sharpie Acrylic Creative Markers were bright, bold, and clear.
Content: My family uses acrylic paint markers for a variety of reasons, and I've never really found a brand that I love--they tend to bleed through, some can't layer without becoming muddy, and priming them is annoying as they tend to have an abrupt splotch/blot of color. I was really excited to get a chance to test this acrylic marker from Sharpie out as they claim to layer well, not bleed through, and not need priming, so thank you to the Stellar Product Testing Panel for giving me these Sharpie Acrylic Creative Markers to try! I'll cut to the chase: I found them to be exactly as advertised. I loved them so much in the 5 pack I received to test that I immediately went and ordered the 12 pack they also have available after I tried them out.They didn't bleed through on any of the papers I tried (standard printer, card stock, glossy papers, etc.), and could layer on top of other colors when dry. They dried very quickly on everything except for the glossy/slick materials--even on these they didn't have a long dry time and didn't budge once dried. Even on dark paper the Sharpie Acrylic Creative Markers were bright, bold, and clear. I cannot overstate how much I loved that they didn't need priming--anyone who uses paint markers has probably had the misfortune to have a blotch of paint come out when priming, but the Sharpie Acrylic Markers didn't have that problem at all. I loved that.Finally, they cleaned off of my skin with basic soap, water, and a bit of handwashing. No problem at all! I'm very happy with them and will be a customer going forward

Content:
For the price, these are excellent paint pens. They function about how you'd expect - they're lightweight so easy to hold, they have quite vibrant colors, and they will work on many surface types. I'm using them on a light, unstained wood, and I have to use at least two coats of whatever color I'm using. That being said, the end product is going to look really nice.

The case they come in is not the best, so I would recommend planning for an alternate storage solution. I purchased a separate pen/pencil case for them that will hold them horizontally as is recommended from the product for how to store them.

The fine side writes really fine and nice. The thicker side is all good. If you go in swirls, you can't really see the strokes. That said, I go side to side because I like the look of strokes because it really screams hand painted. You will need to leave whatever project it is to sit and dry. It's still paint, and as such needs to dry. If you grab it right after, you will get paint on yourself. Thus, if you're getting these for children, I would recommend close supervision. Otherwise, I can see people of most ages really enjoying these for art projects, and especially those who may find it difficult to hold certain brushes or those who don't have storage space for lots of brush types, palettes, etc. Paint pens are a nice alternative.

You can paint over your mistakes after they've dried. I have tested that because I don't have the steadiest hand, so I make mistakes often. However, I have not tried to correct a lighter color over a darker color. Only dark over light, so be mindful that it's paint. It will bleed or blend together. Would not recommend for single-use/one-day projects. Most projects with these will need multiple days. I could see this being fun for really unique beading designs if you're making household decor, crafts, jewelry, etc.

Content: This set of 80 acrylic paint pens earns a mixed review.  The pens are neatly packaged in a sturdy and organized zipper case.  This makes storing the pens horizontally easy and ensures your art area is not messy.  I laid out the case and took a piece of pre-cut 4X6-inch white cardstock.  I attempted to start drawing with the black pen.  I couldn’t get the cap off the paint pen.  I eventually had to get a rubber gripper that is used to remove jar lids.  I got into a rhythm and was soon able to remove the tops off the sample pens I tried as I drew my drawing.  I needed to twist and pull using the rubber gripping pad.  If you have arthritis, you may have to work around the fact that the tops are incredibly difficult to get off the paint pens.I started with the black pen, creating a basic drawing to fill in with different colors.  First, I used traditional paint markers to fill in the petals of the flowers.  Then, I used several metallic markers to fill in the flower center and leaves.  Finally, I touched up the black ink and attempted to do some detail work.  I colored the four blue corners last.  The three white dots in those corners took three coats with the white acrylic paint marker.  In contrast, the whitish/grey coloring on the stems is one coat with the white marker (see photograph).The paint pens dry fairly quickly.  I got several paint spots on my hands, which I cleaned with a scrub brush, warm water, and hand soap.  The black pen easily covered minimal mistakes made while coloring the petals and center.  I had to use a light touch, or the nib would wear away my paper. I used a metallic pen to color the center of the flowers. The paint flow was too heavy and made a mess when I opened it.  Eventually, that particular marker’s paint flow slowed, and I could continue to use it.I decided to test whether these paint pens are waterproof and quick-drying.  I waited fifteen minutes after I was done with the drawing.  I wetted down a paper towel with three squirts of water and dragged it two times across the right-hand side of the drawing.  The ink did not smear on the paper but lifted off and covered my paper towel (see photograph).  I have concerns about using these paint pens on anything exposed to water.  Paint from both the regular and metallic pens was present on the paper towel.On another 4X6-inch piece of cardstock, I used two colors to write letters, numbers, and common words  (see photograph).  As you can see, the medium-sized nibs make detailed drawing and writing difficult.  The manufacturer does not hide this; few examples of tiny writing or detailing are on the product description page.  Additional acrylic pens to finish your artwork may be necessary, depending on what you are creating.This paint pen set is much better than others I have tried, but it misses the mark with caps that can’t be easily removed and paint that is not waterproof.  Even with that in mind, I believe this is still a good value for 80-paint pens.  This set may work for you if you are a doodler and want to have fun.  However, if you are serious about your art, you may need to look elsewhere to be completely satisfied.

Sentence: Unfortunately, my particular box of markers contained two of T329 and missing T333, which I didn't notice until I was in the process of testing them and transferring to a new holder.
Content: Unfortunately, my particular box of markers contained two of T329 and missing T333, which I didn't notice until I was in the process of testing them and transferring to a new holder. I was only given the option to request a return and replacement and ultimately decided against it since I had already started using them. I have my concerns about the delicacy and endurance of the marker nibs. I probably will not use them on anything rougher than cardstock and I'm not sure they would hold up against use on wood or stone unless they are extremely smooth or polished surfaces, but I will admit that I did not attempt this.With that being said, these have to be the best quality acrylic markers I have yet to use. They went on my cardstock paper consistently, smoothly and the colors are still vibrant after drying with no clumping, bumps or bubbles. The paint seems to take other mediums layered over the top well, such as outlining markers. The individual marker caps click to indicate they are closed in a very satisfying way, feeling secure but not overly difficult to open. While not a functional part of the markers, I also really enjoy the clear section where you can see the paint inside.While I am a little disappointed by the missing color from my order, I still would consider purchasing these markers again.

Sentence: I painted small squares of each color with only one coast of paint on both white and black papers and have attached a picture to this review.
Content: I have tried about half a dozen brands of acrylic brush markers and these are among the very best.  I like the selection of colors (I got the set of 36) and have tried them all.  All the colors have good to excellent coverage.  I painted small squares of each color with only one coast of paint on both white and black papers and have attached a picture to this review.  As you can see, the colors with only once rapid coat covers completely (the white spots in some of the colors are only because I missed; I did not want to go back and fill in those spots because then I would create a second coat in some areas).  The coverage for black is very good considering how thin the acrylic ink is for one coat.  If you go over the paint a second time the colors are as vibrant as the ones painted on white paper.  I do wish there were names on the colors, but I guess names are just names and the best way to determine which color you want is to base your selection on the paint brush itself.  The covers on the pens are very close to the actual color but not quite exact; I recommend looking at the nib.  I will be using these pens often.

Sentence: They are easy to layer overtop of each other so if you make a mistake it’s easy to fix and they’re vibrant.I like that the kit comes with extra felt tips and number stickers so the box can stay organized.
Content: This is my first experience using / buying acrylic markers like these. I’m really impressed overall with the amount of colors you get for the low price. Normal professional markers are more than triple the price for a third of the amount. The darker colors are more opaque and some of the colors were already a bit dried out. But that’s not a deal breaker for me. I like the dual tip as well. This set also comes with twelve iridescent markers that are very opaque. The gold is literally liquid gold. I did my first drawing of this turtle and I’m really happy overall. They are easy to layer overtop of each other so if you make a mistake it’s easy to fix and they’re vibrant.I like that the kit comes with extra felt tips and number stickers so the box can stay organized. I did do four stars just because some of the colors were already not usable straight out of the box.

And have scotch tape handy, cause the number stickers don’t stay on.

Content: Decent quality for the price. There is a nice range of shades including 24 metallics. This is a great starter, good value and definitely gets the job done. Set comes with color chart and numbered label stickers that you stick on to the markers yourself and a few replacement tips. Sentence:
Maybe they were supposed to be included but they got switched for the ones I received duplicates of?
Finally, they come with stickers so you can label them by number.
Content:
I wanted to love these markers, but there are a few things about them that disappointed me.

First, I received 3 markers that had duplicates of the exact same color. I can see how this happened: the markers have no color names or numbers printed on them. So it was probably easy for the person who initially packed them to make that mistake. With such a wide color range, some colors look very similar to others.
Second, the quality of the markers is not consistent from color to color. Some of them flow nicely with rich, vibrant color. Some of them feel dried out and do not flow well at all. The metallic colors seemed to be the best as far as the paint flow.
I found it surprising that with 120 different colors, some pretty basic colors were not included. For example, there is no navy blue or maroon. Maybe they were supposed to be included but they got switched for the ones I received duplicates of?
Finally, they come with stickers so you can label them by number. But the stickers are garbage and they fall off instantly. It’s odd that the manufacturer doesn’t just assign each color a number and have it printed on the marker.

The carrying case is very nice quality and like I said, some of the markers work beautifully. I am going to keep them because I’m too lazy to return them. I think I will get use out of some of them.

Content:
I wanted to love these markers, but there are a few things about them that disappointed me.

First, I received 3 markers that had duplicates of the exact same color. I can see how this happened: the markers have no color names or numbers printed on them. So it was probably easy for the person who initially packed them to make that mistake. With such a wide color range, some colors look very similar to others.
Second, the quality of the markers is not consistent from color to color. Some of them flow nicely with rich, vibrant color. Some of them feel dried out and do not flow well at all. The metallic colors seemed to be the best as far as the paint flow.
I found it surprising that with 120 different colors, some pretty basic colors were not included. For example, there is no navy blue or maroon. Maybe they were supposed to be included but they got switched for the ones I received duplicates of?
Finally, they come with stickers so you can label them by number. But the stickers are garbage and they fall off instantly. It’s odd that the manufacturer doesn’t just assign each color a number and have it printed on the marker.

The carrying case is very nice quality and like I said, some of the markers work beautifully. I am going to keep them because I’m too lazy to return them. I think I will get use out of some of them.

Content:
Absolutely love these. I originally bought the 72ct. After a couple months I decided I liked them well enough to buy the 130ct. For a larger variety.
(First pic is of the 2 sets side by side without the opposite sides of the fold out sections.)

There’s a couple differences between the 2 sets outside of the obvious color range. The 72ct came with just the markers in the case. I expected the same from the 130ct however I was pleasantly surprised to find a baggy of replacement nibs and instructions on how to replace said nibs as well as instructions on how to fix them if they become dried out.

Pros:
- Easy control
- Smooth consistency and flow.
- Juicy
- Bright, bold, vibrant, gorgeous colors.
- If your main qualifier is brush tips these are perfect! Capable of creating thick lines but also capable of creating those fine details as well as get into the smaller nooks and crannies.
- layer well with like colors.
- No smudging or smearing.
- Dry quickly
- Fine tip is great for dotting. I’ve used them primarily for adding dots and other embellishments over top blocks of color.
- Case is well made and makes for easy storage as well as taking them on the go.
- good color variety in both sets making smooth and subtle color transitions a breeze.
- NO BLEEDING

Cons:
- 3 of the markers in the 72ct arrived dry, however not entirely. (Upon receiving instructions in the larger set in how to fix this I feel this has been made up, tho these instructions should be included in the smaller sets.)
- The fine point is not very fine, it is indeed a small bullet tip that doesn’t do well at all for fine details. The brush tip works better.
- There is some color consistency issues between the brush and bullet tip on some colors however slight.
- Some of the fine tips leave behind fibers.
- These do NOT work well on fabrics, colors will not show.
- Majority of the colors do not appear well on black surfaces. (This does not seem to be the case coloring over lines in coloring books).
- Not all colors layer nicely as these are water based, if you attempt to layer colors on opposite sides of the spectrum they just mix.
- There is only one Red in the 72ct.
- Some colors are more transparent than opaque in the fine tip.

Overall, very worth it. I have sets Ive paid more for that were far less quality.

**All NON metallic colors used in my posted photos are from these 2 sets.**

Sentence: I primed some ink on the tape and it stayed wet long enough to dip a wet paintbrush in the ink and smear it onto the watercolor paper that my sketch was on.
Content:
These paint pens are simply fabulous! Not a marker or a pen, but actually paint in a pen. So much fun to play around with! I had just sketched out a little scene from Pinterest, trying to decide if I wanted to purchase the stamp set. Since it was just sitting there I decided to use these paint pens … FYI, I had a blast and was pleasantly surprised.

First you have to prime each pen to get the paint flowing. Originally I had used a permanent ink sketching pen to do this and I was pretty amazed that these paint pens are opaque and could completely cover my black sketching ink. I purposely left some of the black in showing, but I could have covered it if I had wanted too.

I discovered a fun little hack. On the paper towels I was using to prime these pens, I also had a piece of clear scotch tape. I primed some ink on the tape and it stayed wet long enough to dip a wet paintbrush in the ink and smear it onto the watercolor paper that my sketch was on. An improvised paint pallet! I had to move quickly, but it was doable.

When you prime these paint pens, use multiple layers of paper towel as the ink is permanent and you dont want to mark up your work surface. I got these to use on wooden Christmas ornaments with my grandkids so we will all be wearing painting aprons to protect our clothes.

I found this set to be so much fun to use. Just remember that this really is paint flowing out of a pen. It dries quickly. The metallics are especially sparkly. Any artsy kid or adult would love this set!
